title: In-situ observation of precipitation and austenite reversion in additively manufactured 18 wt. % Ni maraging steel
abstract: Maraging steel with 18 wt.% Ni (Mar18Ni) has attracted growing interest for additive manufacturing (AM), particularly through powder bed fusion with a laser beam (PBF-LB), owing to its high strength and heat-treatability. However, the microstructural characteristics introduced by PBF-LB can significantly influence phase transformation pathways during post-processing. While conventionally processed maraging steels have been extensively studied, the precipitation behavior and austenite reversion kinetics in AM-produced Mar18Ni steel remain insufficiently understood. This study investigates the phase transformations in PBF-LB Mar18Ni steel using in-situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM). Samples were subjected to isothermal aging at 480 °C and austenite reversion heat treatments at 650 and 670 °C. The evolution of intermetallic precipitates and the nucleation and morphological development of austenite were systematically characterized. The first precipitation sequence involved Fe2(Mo,Ti) and Ni3Mo after ∼1 h at 480 °C, followed by Ni3Ti formation after a crystallographic rearrangement between martensite and austenite. Unlike the conventionally processed alloy, Ni3Mo forms prior to Ni3Ti in this PBF-LB steel. During aging, precipitation initially competes with austenite reversion as Fe, Ni, and Ti are consumed from the matrix, reducing austenite stability. With prolonged exposure, however, austenite persists and coarsens. At 650 °C, twinning-mediated reversion begins after ∼12 min, whereas at 670 °C, reversion proceeds entirely via the Kurdjumov-Sachs orientation relationship. Al-Ti-rich nano-oxides act as preferential heterogeneous nucleation sites for austenite, promoting reversion but limiting further precipitation. Overall, the results reveal a thermokinetic balance between precipitation and reversion in PBF-LB Mar18Ni steel, providing mechanistic insight into its microstructural evolution.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Maraging steels, particularly the Mar18Ni grade 300 due to its exceptional mechanical strength after aging, are precipitation-hardened alloys widely used in aerospace, tooling, and high-performance structural applications due to their remarkable combination of strength and toughness [ 1 , 2 ]. Their microstructure typically consists of a dislocated martensitic matrix [ 3 ], which serves as a substrate for the precipitation of intermetallics such as Laves phases, e.g., Fe 2 (Mo,Ti), Fe 2 Mo, and Fe 2 Ti [ 4 ], Ni 3 Ti, and Ni 3 Mo [ 5 , 6 ] during aging heat treatment. These dispersed precipitates are responsible for the superior mechanical properties observed in this class of steels [ 7 , 8 ].

The adoption of powder bed fusion with a laser beam (PBF-LB) technique for processing maraging steels has opened new design and manufacturing possibilities, but it also introduces substantial microstructural complexity [ 9 ]. The steep thermal gradients and rapid solidification inherent to metal additive manufacturing processes involving powders and a laser beam [ 10 ] result in far-from-equilibrium microstructures characterized by retained austenite [ 11 ], chemical segregation [ 12 ], and the formation of intermetallics such as Laves phases, whose presence depends on the local Ti and Mo contents [ 13 ]. Moreover, nano-oxides enriched in Al and Ti have been reported in additively manufactured maraging steels, potentially influencing both precipitation kinetics and phase transformation mechanisms during post-processing heat treatments [ 14 , 15 ].

Post-build heat treatments are applied to optimize the microstructure and mechanical performance of PBF-LB maraging steels. Aging at temperatures close to 480 °C promotes the precipitation of strengthening intermetallics [ 16 ], whereas higher temperature treatments between 610 and 670 °C can induce the reversion of martensite into austenite, especially in regions enriched in gamma-stabilizing elements such as Ni [ 17 , 18 ]. However, the interplay between these processes remains poorly understood in the PBF-LB Mar18Ni steel, particularly regarding the competition between precipitate formation and austenite stabilization [ 19 ], and how this is influenced by local chemistry and the presence of nano-oxides.

Investigating the precipitation phenomena via direct aging heat treatment conducted at 490 °C for 3 h, i.e., without prior annealing, in Mar18Ni steel samples processed by PBF-LB, Mei et al. (2022) [ 8 ] observed the emergence of acicular austenite-like morphologies within martensitic laths. This phase exhibited an orientation relationship (OR) with the martensitic matrix consistent with the Nishiyama-Wassermann model after the heat treatment. In addition, acicular precipitates displaying Fe and Co depletion were reported and identified as Ni-rich intermetallics, such as hexagonal close-packed Ni 3 Ti and orthorhombic Ni 3 Mo. The precipitation behavior in conventionally processed Mar18Ni steel has also been investigated, with a focus on the role of molybdenum in the formation of Ni 3 Ti intermetallics. In the study by Niu et al. (2023) [ 20 ], the absence of Mo in the alloy proved detrimental, as it led to the formation of coarse Ni 3 Ti precipitates associated with precipitate-free zones (PFZs) along martensitic grain boundaries, which compromised the mechanical strength of the alloy. On the other hand, the presence of only 3 wt. % Mo promoted its segregation at grain boundaries, which in turn refined the Ni 3 Ti precipitates and enhanced boundary cohesion, ultimately improving the mechanical performance. Although the study by Fonseca et al. (2023) [ 4 ] was conducted on a maraging 400 steel containing 13 wt. % Ni, the authors also explored the role of molybdenum in the precipitation behavior. It was found that, after the formation of Ni-based intermetallics, stable Laves phase clusters such as Fe 2 (Mo,Ti) were uniformly distributed throughout the microstructure. Furthermore, the authors reported that during the aging heat treatment, dislocation rearrangement and the formation of martensitic subgrains occurred simultaneously with precipitation, which preferentially nucleated in regions previously occupied by dislocation tangles.

In the study by Feitosa et al. (2022) [ 17 ], the phenomenon of austenite reversion in conventionally processed maraging 350 steel with 18 wt. % Ni was investigated. The authors found that nickel plays a leading role in the austenite reversion process, as it was the only element whose concentration in the austenite phase decreased with increasing reversion temperature in the range of 610 to 670 °C. Additionally, they indirectly observed that the growth of reverted austenite promotes both the consumption of martensite and the dissolution of intermetallic precipitates, as evidenced by a reduction in hardness. Studying the morphology of reverted austenite in the same alloy subjected to a reversion heat treatment at 640 °C for durations ranging from 1 to 8 h, Viswanathan et al. (2005) [ 18 ] identified austenite with various morphologies, including Widmanstätten, globular, recrystallized, and island-like. The authors also highlighted nickel as the key element in stabilizing the reverted austenite. They indicated it as a primary factor responsible for delaying precipitation due to its preferential dissolution into the austenite phase. In a more recent study by Feitosa et al. (2024) [ 19 ], which investigated the same alloy subjected to identical austenite reversion heat treatment protocols, the authors reported that the nucleation of reverted austenite induces internal stresses within the martensitic matrix; however, its subsequent growth is accompanied by stress relaxation, attributed to recovery mechanisms. Moreover, the kinetics of austenite formation were found to be facilitated by the presence of retained austenite originating from the fabrication route. At temperatures up to 650 °C, precipitates tend to coalesce, while in the range of 650 to 700 °C, their progressive dissolution provides solute elements, such as Ni, Ti, and Mo, which diffuse into the austenite phase and promote its growth. Accordingly, the authors suggest a dual role of intermetallic precipitates during austenite reversion: acting as nucleation facilitators at the early stages and subsequently being depleted to sustain the growth of the reverted austenite.

Although the studies above have addressed precipitation and austenite reversion phenomena in maraging steels processed either by PBF-LB or by conventional routes, none have systematically investigated these phase transformations via in-situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM). Therefore, the present study aims to elucidate the microstructural evolution of Mar18Ni steel produced by PBF-LB during both direct aging and austenite reversion. To this end, in-situ TEM was employed to monitor phase transformations in real-time during post-processing heat treatments conducted at 480 °C for 3 h and at 650 and 670 °C for 45 min. The investigation focused on identifying precipitate phases and their orientation relationships with the martensitic matrix and austenite, characterizing the formation and evolution of austenite variants, and assessing the influence of Al and Ti-oxides and chemical segregation on the transformation pathways.

sections.heading: Mar18Ni steel processing
paragraphs:
Gas-atomized Mar18Ni steel powder was processed using a commercial EOS M280 system via powder bed fusion with a laser beam (PBF-LB) under a nitrogen-protected atmosphere. Processing parameters included a laser power of 180 – 200 W, a beam spot diameter of 100 – 120 μm, a scanning speed of 1 m/s, a hatch spacing of 100 μm, and a layer thickness of 50 μm, all of which were kept constant throughout the build. The chemical composition of the PBF-LB processed parts, as determined by optical emission spectroscopy for metallic elements extracted from a previous study [ 21 ], and by inert gas fusion for oxygen and nitrogen, is included in  Table 1 
                          to provide a better context for the reader.

sections.heading: Scanning electron microscopy characterization and CALPHAD calculations
paragraphs: Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) analyses were conducted on the cross-section perpendicular to the build direction of Mar18Ni steel samples produced by PBF-LB in the as-built (AB) condition and after isothermal heat treatments consisting of aging at 480 °C for 3 h and austenite reversion at 650 °C for 30 min and 670 °C for 30 min, all performed without prior annealing and followed by air cooling to room temperature. The objective was to investigate possible microstructural changes induced by the heat treatments. The analyses were carried out using a Thermo Scientific Quattro Environmental Field Emission Gun (FEG) SEM at the Center for Electron Microscopy and Analysis (CEMAS), The Ohio State University. The detailed surface preparation procedure is described in [ 21 ]. To complement the investigation of phase transformations in Mar18Ni steel as a function of temperature and the compositional evolution of austenite under distinct temperatures, thermodynamic calculations were performed using the CALPHAD module of Thermo-Calc® 2023b (TCFE9 database), based on the chemical composition reported in  Table 1 .

sections.heading: In-situ transmission electron microscopy and data analysis
paragraphs:
Three lamellae of Mar18Ni steel produced through PBF-LB were prepared using a focused ion beam (FIB) system in a Thermo Fisher Scientific Helios NanoLab 660 dual-beam scanning electron microscope, located at the Brazilian Nanotechnology National Laboratory (LNNano) of the Brazilian Center for Research in Energy and Materials (CNPEM). A schematic representation of the section from which the lamellae were extracted (gray-shaded plane), indicating the scanning direction (SD), transverse direction (TD), and PBF-LB building direction (BD), was added to  Fig. 1 
                         . The lamellae were mounted on DENS solutions  wildfire  in-situ heating chips and subsequently loaded onto a double-tilt holder, as depicted in  Fig. 1 (a)-(c), for analysis in a Thermo Fisher/FEI Titan Cubed Themis transmission electron microscope (TEM), also housed at LNNano/CNPEM.

TEM analyses were conducted at 300 kV under both convergent beam (high-angle annular dark-field imaging, HAADF, and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDXS)) and parallel beam conditions (selected area electron diffraction, SAED; bright field, BF, and dark field, DF, imaging). Initially, each lamella was characterized at room temperature in distinct regions to identify and analyze the phases and their chemical compositions in the as-built condition at the nanoscale. Subsequently, the lamellae were subjected to isothermal heat treatments to investigate the phase transformations upon heating. The heating and cooling ramps were standardized to 60 s to reach the target temperature and return to 22 °C, respectively, across all experiments. As illustrated in  Fig. 1 (d)-(f), the first lamella underwent an aging heat treatment at 480 °C for approximately 3 h. The second and third lamellae were subjected to austenite reversion at 650 °C and 670 °C, respectively, for 45 min.

The aging temperature of 480 °C was selected because it lies within the classical precipitation-strengthening regime of maraging steels, where rapid hardness increase is achieved within short aging times, followed by a plateau after few hours . Previous studies have shown that aging at this temperature promotes the formation of fine intermetallics, with limited additional hardening beyond approximately 3 h, indicating that precipitation strengthening is already well established. Lower aging temperatures require substantially longer times to reach peak hardness, whereas higher temperatures increase the extension of austenite reversion, which may interfere with the analysis of precipitation phenomena [ 7 ].

On the other hand, austenite reversion temperatures of 650 °C and 670 °C were selected to promote isothermal austenite reversion governed by Ni partitioning, while suppressing premature transformation during heating and minimizing austenite instability during subsequent cooling. Lower reversion temperatures are associated with sluggish kinetics and require longer soaking times, whereas temperatures above this range may lead to destabilization of austenite during cooling due to insufficient solute partitioning [ 17 ].

The plots were generated from temperature data recorded by the DENS solutions  Impulse  software during in-situ TEM experiments as the heat treatments were applied. The system was calibrated using a linear coefficient of 0.001779, which was applied to convert the electrical power input into the corresponding temperature values. Following aging and each austenite reversion heat treatment, SAED, EDXS mapping, and imaging were performed to assess the phase transformations. Phase identification was performed by calculating the interplanar spacings and comparing them to the corresponding crystallographic ICSD reference files for martensite 64795, austenite 44862, Fe 2 Mo 632626, Fe 2 Ti 107646, Ni 3 Ti 30216, Ni 3 Mo 105046, Al 2 O 3  (corundum) 9770, and TiO 2  (rutile) 9161.

sections.heading: Results and discussion
paragraphs:
The results of the first region of interest (ROI-1), before aging, are presented in  Fig. 2 
                      (a)-(c). Initially, only martensite (in yellow) and austenite (in red), which formed at high processing temperatures and did not transform into martensite upon cooling, were identified, as confirmed by the SAED pattern in  Fig. 2 (a) [ 22 ]. The diffraction spot marked by the dashed circle corresponds to the dark field (DF) image in  Fig. 2 (b), which reveals fine non-identified phases dispersed within a martensite lath. In the study by Kürnsteiner et al. (2023) [ 13 ], a ternary model of maraging steel based on the composition [Fe–19Ni] 1 – x  Ti x , with 0 <  x  < 21 at. %, was fabricated using the directed energy deposition (DED) process. Without any post-processing heat treatment, the authors reported the formation of Fe 2 Ti-type Laves phase in the AB condition when the Ti content reached approximately 5 at. %. These intermetallics were shown to form at the expense of both martensite and austenite, as the depletion of Ti from the austenite phase destabilizes it. The Laves phases are fine and challenging to characterize due to their formation during solidification, driven by Ti rejection from the liquid phase and subsequent segregation into intercellular regions. These regions, enriched in Ti, promote the simultaneous development of both retained austenite and Laves-type intermetallics, which help to explain the presence of the sub-nanometric particles dispersed within the martensite laths observed in  Fig. 2 (b). Although such phases have been reported in the literature for this steel processed by AM in the as-built condition, the superlattice spots in this SAED pattern did not correspond to these intermetallics. Nonetheless, before the formation of fully developed Fe 2 (Mo, Ti)-type Laves phases, through aging heat treatment, nanoscale solute-enriched regions, and chemically heterogeneous clusters can be present in the as-built Mar18Ni steel microstructure, as evidenced in  Fig. 2 (a) and (b) for ROI-1. These entities lack a well-defined crystal structure and, therefore, make their characterization by SAED intrinsically challenging. During subsequent aging, they evolve through solute redistribution and growth, ultimately leading to the formation of identifiable Laves-phase precipitates [ 16 ]. The EDXS maps acquired from the region depicted in the HAADF image of  Fig. 2 (c) show strong enrichment of Fe, Ni, and Co in a grain-like area where retained austenite is present, indicating chemical segregation that promotes the stabilization of this phase [ 16 ]. Additionally, Al, Ti, and O-enriched particles were identified; nevertheless, the superlattice spots observed in the background of this SAED pattern could not be indexed to either corundum or rutile structures of the oxide phases.

After approximately 1 h of isothermal aging, the SAED pattern in  Fig. 2 (j) reveals the formation of Laves phase cluster, Fe 2 (Mo, Ti) (in blue), and Ni 3 Mo (in pink), which were not previously detected in ROI-1. The formation of Laves-phase clusters in this region is likely associated with the evolution of nanoscale solute-enriched sites inherited from the as-built microstructure [ 16 ], which exhibited limited crystallographic order preceding aging, rendering their identification by SAED particularly challenging. The DF images in  Fig. 2 (k) and (l), corresponding to DF I  and DF II , respectively, confirm that both intermetallic phases are ultrafine and distributed throughout the martensitic matrix.  Fig. 2 (m) presents a bright-field (BF) image of the same region to highlight that, despite the small size of the nanoprecipitates, they exhibit various types of fringe contrast, either parallel to the defined x or y-axes or oriented obliquely. Among these, oblique fringes are the most observed, supporting the presence of interfacial dislocations and the semicoherent nature of the precipitates, as previously reported in the literature [ 7 , 23 ]. Furthermore, EDXS maps acquired from the same region depicted in  Fig. 2 (c), after 2 h and 50 min of aging, reveal that the enrichment of Fe, Ni, and Co previously observed in austenitic regions has diminished, consistent with the precipitation of Fe 2 (Mo, Ti) and Ni 3 Mo. Aluminum, titanium, and oxygen remain associated with the nanoparticles described as metal-rich oxides, with no significant changes in their spatial distribution during the aging treatment.

Fig. 2 (d)-(f) present the results obtained for ROI-2 prior to aging. The SAED pattern in  Fig. 2 (d) reveals the presence of martensite and retained austenite phases. The retained austenite tends to be located within the martensitic laths as isolated island-like regions. In addition, part of this phase is also distributed along the lath boundaries, as evidenced by the DF image in  Fig. 2 (e). The HAADF image in  Fig. 2 (f), along with the corresponding elemental maps, reveals the presence of Al, Ti, and O-rich particles and regions exhibiting both enrichment and depletion of Fe, Ni, and Co, consistent with observations in ROI-1.

After approximately 1 h and 25 min of isothermal aging, the SAED pattern shown in  Fig. 2 (n) reveals the nucleation and/or growth of new phases not previously indexed in ROI-2, including Ni 3 Ti (in white) and the Laves phases Fe 2 (Mo,Ti), alongside previously identified martensite and austenite. The Laves phases Fe 2 (Mo,Ti) were formed during aging, as confirmed both by SAED indexing and indirectly by EDXS maps derived from the HAADF image in  Fig. 2 (q), acquired after 2 h and 30 min of heat treatment. These maps reveal a localized depletion of Ti and Mo compared to their initial distribution, indicating that they were redistributed from the matrix to form nanoprecipitates, rather than remaining concentrated in austenite, as previously reported [ 4 ]. The region highlighted by the dashed circle DF I  in the SAED pattern corresponds to the DF I  image in  Fig. 2 (o), which shows localized enrichment of austenite, primarily along martensitic lath boundaries. The second region, marked by the dashed circle DF II , corresponds to a martensitic lath in which precipitates, such as Ni 3 Ti, had nucleated, alongside darker contrast regions identified as austenite in  Fig. 2 (p). The interfaces between martensite and austenite identified in DF II  also exhibit Ni 3 Ti precipitation. This observation suggests that at relatively low temperatures, such as the 480 °C aging condition, Ni and Ti atoms diffusing from the austenite phase promote the nucleation and growth of Ni 3 Ti precipitates within the adjacent martensitic matrix through a heterogeneous nucleation mechanism. In this context, phase interfaces act as nucleation sites, as they inherently represent surface defects and typically present linear defects that accommodate the strain arising from the structural mismatch between the phases [ 18 ]. The HAADF image in  Fig. 2 (q) and the corresponding EDXS maps indicate that the enrichment of Fe, Ni, and Co appears to have decreased compared to the pre-aging condition, as these elements are more homogeneously distributed. This is likely due to their partitioning from the austenite phase into the formation of strengthening intermetallic precipitates. Al, Ti, and O-rich particles remain present in the region, and the overall elemental composition does not appear to have changed at the spatial resolution accessible by EDXS.

Fig. 2 (g)-(i) present the microstructural and compositional analysis of ROI-3 before heat treatment. The SAED pattern in  Fig. 2 (g) confirms the presence of martensite and retained austenite from the PBF-LB process. The DF image in  Fig. 2 (h) shows that the diffraction spots highlighted by the dashed circle in the SAED pattern originate from the

In this ROI, the superlattice spots in the background of the SAED pattern in  Fig. 2 (g) were indexed to the Al 2 O 3  phase, corundum-type structure, as illustrated by the unit cell outlined in green. EDXS maps collected from the HAADF image depicted in  Fig. 2 (i) also confirm the presence of Al, Ti, and O-enriched particles, and as already observed, regions enriched in Fe, Ni, and Co.

After approximately 2 h of isothermal aging, the SAED pattern in  Fig. 2 (r) shows that previously identified martensite and austenite phases remain present. During aging, the formation of a new phase was observed: the Ni 3 Mo intermetallic. According to the time-temperature-transformation (TTT) diagrams for conventionally processed maraging 300 steels, Ni 3 Mo and Ni 3 Ti are the first intermetallics to nucleate during aging [ 6 ]. Furthermore, the Fe 2 (Mo,Ti) Laves cluster and the Ni 3 Mo phases, as shown in the DF II  image in  Fig. 2 (t), consist of uniformly dispersed ultrafine precipitates that occupy a substantial portion of the martensitic matrix, indicating a widespread distribution [ 4 ]. On the other hand, the DF I  image in  Fig. 2 (s), corresponding to an austenite indexed spot, reveals this phase dispersed within martensitic laths and at lath boundaries, exhibiting an island-like morphology, as indicated by arrows. Even though the process occurs at a relatively low temperature, in regions of metallic segregation, the austenite start temperature (A s ) can approach the aging temperature (480 °C), enabling the emergence of new austenite nucleation sites in addition to the growth of the retained austenite [ 24 ]. Despite these microstructural changes, the elemental maps derived from  Fig. 2 (u) show no significant variation in the elemental global segregation of ROI-3, except for a slight depletion of Fe, Ni, and Co. The first two are directly associated with the formation of nanoprecipitates during aging, while Co is typically enriched in austenite. This apparent compositional stability arises from the fact that the solute elements involved in precipitation are mainly localized within sub-nanometric regions [ 20 ], which do not substantially affect the global elemental distribution.

It is reasonable to assume that molybdenum-enriched precipitates form during the early stages of aging, as evidenced in the ROI-1 analysis. This is supported by the fact that Mo diffusion in ferrite (activation energy: 238 kJ/mol) is more favorable than that of Ti (activation energy: 272 kJ/mol) [ 23 ]. On the other hand, investigations conducted on a Mar18Ni alloy with a composition similar to that of the material studied here, except cobalt content, which was approximately twice as high, processed via conventional vacuum melting and remelting and subsequently annealed at 820 °C for 1 h, revealed that Ni-Ti intermetallics initially form at 480 °C [ 25 ]. From this phase, Mo-rich precipitates then nucleate and grow. Additionally, it is well established that, during the early stages of aging in conventional maraging steels, Fe and Co atoms form short-range ordered (SRO) structures that tend to expel Ni atoms. Simultaneously, Mo atoms tend to cluster and incorporate residual Fe, Ni, and Ti, giving rise to Fe 2 (Mo, Ti) and Ni 3 Mo intermetallic phases [ 26 ]. Compared to the study mentioned above [ 25 ], since the alloy investigated here contains lower Co, one may expect less extensive formation of Fe-Co SRO regions. As a result, a greater fraction of Ni atoms would remain available to interact with Mo and form Ni-Mo-based intermetallics at earlier stages of precipitation. In ROI-2, Ni-Mo intermetallic precipitates were not observed for up to 1 h and 25 min of aging. However, during this period, the Ni 3 Ti phase was identified. This observation can be explained by the fact that, despite its higher activation energy, Ti may diffuse through the ferrite matrix via pipe diffusion [ 23 , 27 ]. This mechanism facilitates the nucleation and growth of Ni 3 Ti, particularly at high-density dislocation interfaces between the matrix and the austenite or precipitates. Furthermore, this ROI was the only one in which the previously characterized austenite transformed during the heat treatment, maintaining the same zone axis but exhibiting a modified orientation relationship with martensite. This crystallographic rearrangement appeared to favor the nucleation and growth of the Ni 3 Ti intermetallic phase. Given the enhanced mobility of Ti through dislocation cores, it is plausible that Laves-type Fe 2 (Mo,Ti) phases also formed in Ni-depleted regions, where Ni had segregated to form Ni 3 Ti. At longer aging times, as observed in ROI-3, the simultaneous presence of Ni 3 Mo, Fe 2 (Mo,Ti), and austenite suggests that intermetallic formation and growth had not fully consumed the retained austenite, nor had all elements responsible for austenite stabilization yet been partitioned into the strengthening precipitates.

It is worth noting that although austenite was detected in all three ROIs in the AB condition, its evolution during aging exhibited distinct behaviors. In ROI-1 and ROI-3, austenite persisted throughout the in-situ experiment without apparent crystallographic changes. In ROI-2, however, a crystallographic variant of austenite, different from the retained austenite observed in the AB state, was identified after 1 h and 25 min of aging. During the initial 15 min of aging, retained austenite is known to coarsen, leading to an increase in its volume fraction [ 25 ]. Additionally, the partitioning of alloying elements required for precipitate formation may promote new nucleation sites at the expense of pre-existing austenite. These thermokinetic effects may account for the diverse microstructural evolutions observed across the aging durations: in ROI-1 and in ROI-3, retained austenite may have remained stable due to the local chemical environment and strain heterogeneities, even at prolonged exposure times; in ROI-2, new austenite may have nucleated as aging progressed, in agreement with the proposed transformation sequence (

To substantiate the presence of austenite in as-built and heat-treated conditions, ex-situ XRD patterns of the gas-atomized powder, AB, and heat-treated PBF-LB Mar18Ni steel are provided in Fig. S1 in the Supplementary Material.

The heat-treated lamella that underwent austenite reversion at 650 °C for 45 min was also investigated before the in-situ heat treatment, i.e., in the AB condition, across three distinct regions of interest.  Fig. 3 
                      (a)-(c) present the SAED pattern, the DF image corresponding to the dashed circle in the SAED, and the EDXS maps obtained from the mapping window highlighted in the HAADF image for ROI-1.  Fig. 3 (a) reveals the presence of martensite and austenite phases in this region. The DF image shown in  Fig. 3 (b), acquired from the region marked by the dashed circle in the SAED, reveals finely dispersed, unidentified particles within the martensitic matrix, along with island-like austenite, also indicated in the figure, which were not indexed consistently with either Laves phases or oxides. These particles are so small that they are not detected by mass contrast in the HAADF image shown in  Fig. 3 (c).  Fig. 3 (d)-(f) correspond to ROI-2. In the SAED pattern of  Fig. 3 (d), martensite and austenite reflections were indexed. Although the diffraction spot selected for the DF image corresponds to an austenite indexed reflection, the morphology observed in the DF image suggests the presence of sub-nanometric non-identified particles dispersed in the matrix, besides island-like retained austenite embedded within a martensite lath. Finally,  Fig. 3 (g)-(i) display the results for ROI-3. In the SAED pattern shown in  Fig. 3 (g), martensite and austenite were identified, along with a candidate plane for Laves phases. The unit cell could not be defined due to the incompatibility of the spots with the planes of these phases and the absence of sufficiently sharp reflections. However, the DF image in  Fig. 3 (h), acquired from the region highlighted by the dashed circle in the SAED, shows these finely dispersed non-identified particles, similar in size and distribution to those of ROI-2, probably associated with Laves phases. Moreover, regions within the laths and along lath boundaries exhibit stronger diffraction contrast and higher area fraction, likely associated with island-like retained austenite. The EDXS maps derived from the HAADF images in  Fig. 3 (c), (f), and (i), as in the AB ROIs from the lamella subjected to aging at 480 °C, do not provide essential compositional information regarding the unidentified phases, but indicate the presence of nanoparticles enriched in Al, Ti, and O, as well as Fe, Ni, and Co segregation zones.

To investigate the possible influence of non-identified phases inherited from the PBF-LB processing on the microstructure of Mar18Ni steel during austenite reversion heat treatment conducted at 650 °C, ROI-3 was selected for time-resolved analysis.                        reflection, as shown in  Fig. 3 (j 1 )-(m 1 ). Bright-field images acquired from ROI-3 are also displayed in  Fig. 3 (j 3 )-(m 3 ). The SAED patterns in  Fig. 3 (j 1 ) and (k 1 ) reveal that although austenite and martensite remained present in ROI-3 during the initial stages of the heat treatment, at 4 and 12 min, respectively, crystallographic reorientation occurred, likely through a rotation around the same zone axis. Moreover, the early stages of austenite reversion at 650 °C reveal the appearance of characteristic spots of the Fe 2 (Mo,Ti) Laves phases, which persisted throughout the entire experiment. On the other hand, the SAED patterns collected after 12 min of heat treatment, depicted in  Fig. 3 (l 1 ) and (m 1 ), show the appearance of two reflections from the {113} and {022} families of austenite planes represented in dark blue, which are twinned to the original austenite. This twinning is elucidated by the drawing of a mirror symmetry axis passing through the center of the extended edges associated with the {112} and {013} martensite planes. These results suggest that during the first 12 min of heat treatment, the pre-existing austenite domains undergo crystallographic rearrangement and growth. However, no significant nucleation of new austenite grains with distinct orientations occurs during this stage, as no additional diffraction spots were detected. After 12 min of heat treatment, new austenite domains begin to form, exhibiting orientations similar to those of the original austenite due to twinning on martensitic planes. Similar findings have been reported in the literature [ 23 ], where twinning is associated with morphological changes in austenite as the reversion process progresses. Recrystallized (R A ) and Widmanstätten (W A ) austenite morphologies, observed in the DF images of  Fig. 3 (j 2 )-(m 2 ), are formed through twinning mechanisms. An indication of this phenomenon is the Kurdjumov-Sachs orientation relationship observed between the twinned austenite and the surrounding martensite. This transformation can be explained by a shear-controlled mechanism that initially involves only a crystallographic rearrangement, minimizing the energy barrier. As the process evolves, the stored energy is then utilized to accommodate twinning, enabling further growth of the reverted austenite [ 24 ].

The evolution of the austenite area percentage was quantified using the ImageJ freeware [ 28 ]. Segmentation was restricted to recrystallized austenite located within and along the boundaries of the two martensite laths visible in the DF images in  Fig. 3 (j 2 )-(m 2 ), due to the difficulty in isolating the Widmanstätten structures. However, an apparent increase in needle length can be observed as the heat treatment progresses. The percentage area of austenite must not be interpreted as representative of the total percentage surface of this phase in the investigated lamella, given the limited field of probing. The calculated percentual areas of austenite over time were: 0.598 %, 0.618 %, 0.624 %, and 0.677 %. Although the formation of the twinned austenite did not lead to a marked increase in the percentage of this phase, it indicates the emergence of a distinct variant.

After 35 min of heat treatment, as shown in the HAADF image and corresponding EDXS maps in  Fig. 3 (n) collected from ROI-3, nickel segregation is observed along grain boundaries as well as in the brighter regions containing austenite with a globular morphology. The nano-oxides remain enriched in titanium and aluminum.  Fig. 3 (o 1 )-(o 3 ) present the SAED, DF, and BF images of ROI-3 after cooling the TEM chamber to 22 °C. In addition to martensite, both austenite twinned variants are still present, sharing a common axis that intersects the {113} reflections. This spot aligns with the edge of the diffraction pattern in one variant and with the face diagonal in the other. Laves phases were not detected in the SAED pattern shown in  Fig. 3 (o 1 ); however, they may still be present as sub-nanometric domains, as suggested by the presence of faint superlattice spots in the SAED and fine particles in the DF image in  Fig. 3 (o 2 ). In contrast, distinct austenite morphologies can be identified in the same DF image: globular, island-like, recrystallized, and Widmanstätten. It is also worth noting that the BF image shown in  Fig. 3 (o 3 ) highlights a recrystallized austenite grain, as indicated by arrows, further supporting the previous discussion that twinning is associated with both Widmanstätten and recrystallized austenite morphologies.

Results from TEM analysis of the third Mar18Ni steel lamella in the AB condition are shown in  Fig. 4 
                      (a)-(g). In ROI-1, only martensite and retained austenite were detected, as illustrated in  Fig. 4 (a). A reciprocal lattice overlay was included in this figure to emphasize that the region marked by the dashed circle corresponds to the {022} reflection of austenite. The corresponding DF image in  Fig. 4 (b) reveals island-like austenite embedded within a martensite lath, as indicated by arrows. Fringe contrast is observed between the austenite islands and the martensitic matrix, resulting from a well-defined orientation relationship sustained by interfacial dislocations. EDXS maps from the HAADF image in  Fig. 4 (c) confirm the presence of Al and Ti nano-oxides, as well as Fe, Ni, and Co segregation patterns consistent with those previously discussed for other lamellae in the AB condition. In contrast, SAED data from ROI-2, shown in  Fig. 4 (d), display only martensite, and no additional phases could be identified, except for a candidate plane for Al 2 O 3 . Nevertheless,  Fig. 4 (e) shows fine particles in the DF image associated with a weak reflection spot and a particle with a morphology similar to that of the previously identified Al-Ti oxides. The HAADF image of ROI-2 depicted in  Fig. 4 (f) and its corresponding EDXS maps again confirm the presence of nano-oxides and metallic segregation. A specific nano-oxide particle located near a triple point was further analyzed at higher magnification, as shown in  Fig. 4 (g). EDXS mapping of this region reveals an Al and O-rich core surrounded by a Ti-enriched shell [ 14 , 29 ]. The remaining metallic elements, e.g., Fe, Ni, and Co, are depleted at the oxide site, as previously noted. ROI-3 coincided with a martensitic grain boundary, as evidenced by diffuse spots in the SAED of  Fig. 4 (h). In addition to martensite and austenite phases, a faint spot was indexed as a possible candidate lattice point of Al 2 O 3 . The corresponding BF image, depicted in  Fig. 4 (i), shows retained austenite in island-like morphology, as marked by red arrows [ 4 ]. In the upper grain near the boundary, parallel fringe contrast is observed, indicating local crystalline misorientation between the martensite and austenite phases. Notably, dislocation tangles are present in this region, acting to accommodate the crystallographic mismatch between the phases [ 8 ].

Unlike the previous lamella, in which in-situ analyses during austenite reversion at 650 °C focused on a region containing martensite, austenite, and non-identified phases, the in-situ observations for the third lamella during austenite reversion at 670 °C focused on ROI-1, which initially presented only martensite and retained austenite.  Fig. 4 (j 1 )-(n 2 ) present SAED patterns and DF images acquired at different times during the heat treatment. The SAED patterns show no appearance of new diffraction spots throughout the 27 min of austenite reversion at 670 °C, indicating the absence of newly formed intermetallic phases. However, the DF images reveal a progressive increase in the percentage area of austenite up to 18 min in the region outlined by the dashed ellipse. From 18 to 27 min, the diffraction spots corresponding to austenite become more intense, reflecting the continued growth of this phase in the highlighted region. After 35 min of austenite reversion, HAADF images acquired from ROI-2, as shown in  Fig. 4 (o 1 ) and (o 2 ), reveal phenomena consistent with both site-selective and substrate-assisted nucleation. Since austenite was not detected in the SAED pattern of ROI-2 in the as-built condition, this phase nucleated at two distinct locations: a martensitic grain boundary and the interface between martensite and an Al-Ti-rich nano-oxide, supporting the hypothesis of heterogeneous nucleation. This mechanism has also been reported for conventionally processed maraging steels, where heterogeneous nucleation of austenite was attributed to grain boundaries and dislocations at the interfaces between precipitates and the martensitic matrix [ 30 ]. The identity of the newly formed austenite is corroborated by an enrichment of Fe, Ni, and Mo around the oxide particle, which was absent before the austenite reversion heat treatment. In contrast, the oxide remains enriched in Al, Ti, and O, indicating that the stabilization of the austenite is unlikely to result from the diffusion of Ti from the nano-oxide itself, but likely rather from the consumption of previously formed PBF-LB sub-nanometric precipitates during the reversion process, as reported in other studies [ 19 ].

Finally, after the in-situ holder was cooled to a setpoint of 22 °C and the sample temperature was confirmed to be stable, post-heat treatment data from ROI-1 and ROI-3 were collected and are shown in  Fig. 4 (p 1 )-(p 2 ) and (q 1 )-(q 2 ), respectively. Although the SAED pattern in  Fig. 4 (p 1 ) remains practically unchanged, the corresponding DF image in  Fig. 4 (p 2 ) reveals the presence of a newly recrystallized austenite grain in a region previously occupied by a martensite lath in the as-built condition. This indicates that the heat treatment at 670 °C not only promotes the coarsening of pre-existing austenite, as seen in the island-like morphology within a martensite lath, but also facilitates the formation of new recrystallized austenitic grains. In ROI-3, the post-treatment DF image derived from the SAED pattern shown in  Fig. 4 (q 1 ) highlights austenite domains along martensitic grain boundaries and a Widmanstätten-type austenite region. Although no twinning activity was observed in the SAED patterns acquired during the heat treatment at 670 °C, the presence of morphologies typically associated with this phenomenon, i.e., recrystallized and Widmanstätten austenite, was identified in two distinct regions of the lamella after cooling.

Table 2 
                       summarizes the phases, excluding martensite, identified in the three Mar18Ni steel lamellae under various temperature and time conditions, including the AB state, aged (480 °C for 3 h), and submitted to austenite reversion heat treatment (650 and 670 °C for 45 min). The aluminum oxide with corundum-type structure and Al 2 O 3  stoichiometry was not included in the table, nor were the candidate planes identified for this phase and for the Laves phases in certain ROIs of the as-built lamellae. Additionally, the orientation relationships (ORs) between precipitates and martensite or austenite, as well as between austenite and martensite, are presented.

In the as-built condition, retained austenite, referred to as Austenite I, was typically observed across the AB ROIs of lamellae, exhibiting a Kurdjumov-Sachs (K-S) orientation relationship with the martensitic matrix. Three exceptions were identified. In ROI-1 of lamella 2 and ROI-3 of lamella 3, the OR observed does not correspond to those reported in the literature for this alloy, suggesting a possible influence of local features introduced by the PBF-LB processing, such as the presence of unidentified sub-nanometric intermetallics and nano-metal oxide particles, which may induce stresses in the martensitic matrix and alter its orientation with respect to austenite. In ROI-2 of lamella 3, no diffraction reflections corresponding to austenite were identified, indicating its absence or content below the detection threshold. In ROI-3 of lamella 2, a rotated austenite maintaining K-S OR emerged after 4 min of heat treatment at 650 °C and remained stable up to 27 min of heat treatment. This variant underwent a crystallographic rotation relative to the retained austenite observed in the as-built condition, while preserving its diffraction spots and zone axis. A second variant of austenite, designated Austenite II in  Table 2  and exhibiting a K-S OR, was identified after 12 min and is associated with twin-mediated reversion pathways, as discussed previously. Upon cooling and subsequent reanalysis of the same ROI, both austenite variants preserved their twinned orientation relationship. However, a crystallographic rearrangement was detected, which maintained the same K-S orientation relationship despite changes in martensite reflections and zone axis. This rearrangement is indicative of the transformation mechanism and reflects the recrystallized and Widmanstätten-reverted austenite [ 23 , 24 ], as observed in  Fig. 3 (o 2 ) and (o 3 ). These morphologies may induce local stresses within martensitic grains and contribute to orientation distortions, as briefly discussed in the Supplementary Material. During in-situ heating at 670 °C, particularly in ROI-1 of lamella 3, austenite consistently exhibited the K-S OR for up to 27 min, suggesting that a crystallographically invariant transformation mechanism governed the reversion process. This persistence supports the hypothesis that transformation into K-S-related austenite is energetically favorable [ 23 ]. Although no new precipitates or additional austenite variants were detected during this stage, post-cooling analysis revealed the preservation of the K-S orientation relationship, along with the formation of recrystallized austenite grains. These microstructural features suggest that twinning may also have contributed to the transformation mechanism. After 45 min of in-situ heating followed by cooling to 22 °C, ROI-3 displayed the presence of Austenite II with a slightly altered orientation relationship: (200) A //

                      M , [011] A // [011] M . This differs from the austenite variant initially observed in the same region under the as-built condition. Such behavior aligns with literature reports suggesting that austenite formed at 670 °C may partially revert to martensite upon cooling due to its thermodynamic instability [ 17 ], as discussed in Fig. S2 (Supplementary Material), derived from CALPHAD-based thermodynamic calculations. In the present study, this partial reversion appears to have been accompanied by a subtle crystallographic rearrangement, as evidenced by the shift in orientation relationship between austenite and martensite. It is worth noting that the heat treatment carried out at 650 °C was conducted in a region of the lamella where candidate planes of the Laves phases had already been observed; consequently, the appearance of the lattice of these phases in the SAED pattern during the in-situ analysis was most likely due to growth of the pre-existing sites rather than nucleation. This hypothesis is further supported by the fact that austenite reversion at 670 °C was performed in a region devoid of intermetallics originating from the PBF-LB process, and even at this higher temperature, these phases were not detected throughout the heat treatment.

Intermetallic phases, including Fe 2 (Mo,Ti), Ni 3 Mo, and Ni 3 Ti, were identified during the heat treatments. Among these, the Laves-type Fe 2 (Mo,Ti) phases were the most frequently indexed intermetallic across all lamellae. These phases exhibited different orientation relationships with the martensitic matrix, as well as with austenite, such as in ROIs-2 and 3 of lamella 1 (submitted to aging at 480 °C, see  Table 2 ). The predominance of Fe 2 (Mo,Ti) clusters over their binary counterparts (Fe 2 Mo and Fe 2 Ti) is attributed to the co-presence of Mo and Ti in the local chemical environment. This dual presence statistically favors the nucleation of mixed-phase Fe 2 (Mo,Ti) by reducing the strict compositional constraints necessary for the formation of defined stoichiometric compounds. The absence of Fe 2 Ti and Fe 2 Mo as discrete phases can be hypothesized by the interplay between elemental availability and the early-stage transformation pathways. During the initial stages of aging, austenite reversion does not occur extensively; instead, the retained austenite primarily undergoes coarsening. Under these conditions, sufficient Ni remains available in the martensitic matrix to promote the nucleation of Ni-rich precipitates, thereby reducing the driving force for the stabilization of Fe 2 Mo, since Fe 2 Mo does not stabilize because Mo is preferentially captured into Ni-Mo phases before it can effectively bond with Fe. At the same time, although Ti can diffuse through the martensitic matrix via pipe diffusion, the amount of free Ti is limited by the presence of Al-Ti nano-oxides, which sequester this element and hinder the formation of Fe 2 Ti. As a result, neither Fe 2 Mo nor Fe 2 Ti were detected individually, with the chemical environment instead favoring the cooperative clustering of Mo and Ti, leading to the prevalence of Fe 2 (Mo, Ti) Laves-type precipitates [ 23 , 27 ].

Ni 3 Ti precipitates were identified in ROI-2 of lamella 1 and exhibited orientation relationships with both austenite and martensite. This suggests that their nucleation was promoted by local Ni enrichment and the oriented austenite/martensite domains, consistent with previous findings [ 30 ]. These observations align with the DF imaging presented in  Fig. 2 (p), where Ni 3 Ti was located at austenite/martensite interfaces. In contrast, Ni 3 Mo was observed in ROI-1 and ROI-3 of lamella 1 during the aging heat treatment. This precipitation was found either in alignment exclusively with austenite or exhibiting orientation relationships with both martensite and austenite. The ORs determined for Ni 3 Mo relative to martensite differ from those reported in prior studies [ 7 , 23 ], which primarily addressed the substituted phase Ni 3 (Mo,Ti) with a presumed hexagonal structure. In the present study, however, Ni 3 Mo was confirmed to adopt an orthorhombic crystal structure. This observation agrees with previous research on a conventionally processed maraging steel containing 13 wt. % Ni [ 4 ], which also reported orthorhombic Ni 3 Mo but with distinct orientation relationships compared to the ones observed here. Such discrepancies are justifiable, considering significant differences in alloy composition, processing route, and especially the precipitation sensitivity to the as-built microstructure, as demonstrated throughout this paper. Despite its orthorhombic symmetry, Ni 3 Mo exhibited relatively simple orientation relationships with martensite and austenite, suggesting that nucleation and growth were facilitated at boundaries of the martensite laths and interfaces, respectively [ 4 ]. In contrast to Ni 3 Mo, which was detected in both regions where austenite and martensite exhibited a K-S OR, the formation of Ni 3 Ti appears to be sensitive to the presence of austenite with a specific orientation relationship to the martensitic matrix. This was evidenced in the ROI-2 of lamella 1, the only region among those investigated in which retained austenite underwent a crystallographic transformation during aging, involving changes in diffraction reflections within the same zone axis and a concomitant shift in its orientation relationship with martensite. These observations suggest that the local crystallographic compatibility between austenite and martensite plays an important role in enabling Ni 3 Ti precipitation in this PBF-LB alloy [ 30 ].

The occurrence of “NR” (not reported) ORs highlights the novelty of this study. Many of the identified phases have not been extensively characterized in the existing literature, particularly in the context of in-situ TEM analyses of maraging 300 steel fabricated via PBF-LB. The unique thermal history and nanoscale compositional heterogeneities introduced by the additive manufacturing process present challenges to established orientation relationship databases, underscoring the need for updated characterization frameworks. Furthermore, the presence of intermetallic non-identified (N-I) phases in certain SAED patterns is likely attributable to their sub-nanometric size, low volume fraction, and/or to the superposition of diffraction from coexisting phases. These ambiguous reflections warrant further investigation using techniques such as atom probe tomography (APT) or high-resolution scanning transmission electron microscopy (HR-STEM), which enable sub-nanometric compositional and crystallographic resolution [ 20 ].

Although the microstructural characterization of the as-built and heat-treated samples by SEM was one of the first methodological steps in this study, the corresponding results are presented only in  Fig. 5 
                      . As revealed, several previously unreported phenomena occur during the heat treatments, which were monitored in real time and provided insights into the mechanisms governing precipitation and austenite reversion in PBF-LB Mar18Ni steel. In general,  Fig. 5  shows that few microscale morphological changes occur between the solidification microstructure of the AB condition and the aged state, as the cellular solidification substructure remains largely preserved. However, the schematic representation highlights that the nature and location of the nanoscale precipitates depend on the heat treatment time, with the intermetallic phases forming either dispersed throughout the matrix or preferentially along austenite/martensite interfaces. In contrast, the microstructures obtained after austenite reversion differ from the AB condition yet exhibit similar features among themselves, characterized by a vein-like austenite morphology and a significant volume fraction detectable by SEM. Yet, at the nanoscale, differences emerge between the reversion conditions, particularly in the mechanisms and kinetics of austenite formation: at 650 °C, only reorientation of pre-existing austenite occurs within the first minutes, followed by the nucleation of a twinned variant that remains stable throughout the process. In comparison, at 670 °C, reversion proceeds entirely via the Kurdjumov-Sachs orientation relationship between martensite and austenite, with heterogeneous nucleation assisted by Al-Ti-rich nano-oxides. Overall, the schematic in  Fig. 5  summarizes the nanoscale events elucidated in this study, illustrating how the microstructure evolved from the as-built condition through the different heat-treatment routes investigated.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs:
Three lamellae of Mar18Ni steel processed by powder bed fusion with a laser beam were investigated via TEM in the as-built condition and in real time during the following heat treatments: aging at 480 °C for 3 h and austenite reversion at 650 °C and 670 °C for 45 min. Based on the experimental observations and the associated analyses, the following conclusions can be drawn: 
                         
                            • 
                            The precipitation of strengthening intermetallic phases during the aging heat treatment initially competes with the austenite reversion process, as key gamma-stabilizing elements, particularly Fe, Ni, and Ti, are consumed to form intermetallics, depleting the matrix and reducing austenite stability. However, as precipitation progresses, austenite is not fully depleted. This evidence suggests a competitive mechanism between precipitate nucleation and growth, as well as austenite consumption, whereby precipitate nucleation occurs at the expense of austenite. Nevertheless, with continued aging, austenite not only persists but also coarsens, indicating a shift toward cooperative interactions rather than complete consumption. 
                         
                         
                            • 
                            In contrast to the behavior reported for conventionally processed Mar18Ni steel, the first nickel-based intermetallic form in the present PBF-LB alloy was Ni 3 Mo rather than Ni 3 Ti. This inversion is attributed to the lower Co content in the investigated alloy, which likely limits the formation of Fe-Co short-range order and increases the availability of Ni for early Mo-rich precipitation. Additionally, the lower activation energy for Mo diffusion in ferrite favors the formation of Ni 3 Mo. Notably, Ni 3 Ti was only observed after a crystallographic rearrangement that established a specific orientation relationship between austenite and martensite. 
                         
                         
                            • 
                            During austenite reversion at 650 °C, a crystallographic reorientation of austenite occurs within the first 12 min. Beyond this point, a new austenite variant nucleates through a twinning mechanism from the initial austenite. After cooling to room temperature, both variants are retained, and the presence of recrystallized and Widmanstätten morphologies, along with the Kurdjumov-Sachs (K-S) orientation relationship (OR) between austenite and martensite, provides evidence that twinning does take place during the reversion process. 
                         
                         
                            • 
                            Austenite reversion at 670 °C proceeds entirely through the K-S OR with the surrounding martensitic matrix. After 35 min of treatment, the analysis of a region containing Al-Ti-rich nano-oxides revealed that these particles acted as preferential nucleation sites for heterogeneous austenite formation, originating from an ROI that initially contained no retained austenite from processing. This finding is relevant, as it highlights a cooperative role of nano-oxides in promoting austenite reversion, despite their simultaneous effect of depleting titanium from the matrix, thereby limiting the formation of precipitates during aging and compromising austenite stability. Furthermore, the austenite formed at 670 °C in one of the investigated regions underwent subtle crystallographic rearrangements upon cooling to 22 °C, consistent with previous reports that associate the thermodynamic instability of high-temperature austenite with partial transformation back to martensite upon cooling. 
                         
                         
                            • 
                            The selection of a region containing intermetallics originating from the PBF-LB process for austenite reversion at 650 °C, in contrast to the heat treatment at 670 °C performed in an ROI where such sub-nanometric phases were absent, supports the conclusion that austenite reversion does not significantly promote the nucleation of new intermetallic precipitates but instead enhances the coarsening of those already present in this steel, as long as austenite can nucleate and grow.

This study demonstrates that Mar18Ni steels processed by PBF-LB exhibit distinctive phase transformation pathways, kinetics, and microstructural features compared to their conventionally processed counterparts. The findings highlight the potential to optimize PBF-LB parameters to promote austenite reversion while minimizing titanium consumption, thus balancing precipitation hardening and austenite stability through controlled nano-oxide formation and phase interactions.
